title: Three crops of one subject
objective: Choose a crop that makes the relationship between a mug and book read clearly before adding detail.

warmup.instructions: Place a mug beside a book and choose a fixed seat. In seven minutes, sketch two small frames around the same arrangement, changing where the page edges cut it and how much margin it has.

explanation: The edges of your page make a frame, or format, around the mug and book. A closer crop, a shifted crop, or wider margins changes the sizes of the empty spaces as well as the space the objects occupy. There is no universally correct crop; choose the one that makes the relationship you want to show easiest to read.

Keep the arrangement and viewpoint steady while you compare frames. First draw only the large shapes, then inspect the gaps around and between them as in Lesson 3. Watch for accidental near-touches, where an object almost meets another contour or the frame and leaves a narrow, confusing sliver. Pick a crop that gives the forms clear room or cuts an edge decisively.

exercise.instructions:
1. Arrange a mug and closed book in steady light. Choose your viewpoint and leave the objects in place while you compare crops.
2. Draw three small rectangle frames. In each, show only the large shapes of both objects; vary the crop and margins—one generous, one closer, and one shifted toward an edge.
3. Compare the empty spaces around and between the mug and book. Check whether their contours stay clear or make awkward near-touches with each other or the frame.
4. Circle the crop that makes the relationship easiest to read. If needed, adjust the crop slightly to open a gap or give one form more room.
5. Below, draw a larger version of that crop. Place the big shapes first, check the margins and gaps, then add only the details needed to identify the objects.

Source concept: edwards-right-side-brain-concept-03. These pages discuss format edges, how positive and negative shapes fit together, and their role in composition and balance.

Adapted exercise idea: compare a small still-life crop before making a larger drawing. pp. 172–174 address positive and negative shapes, p. 180 cropping, and p. 195 tangencies. The lesson uses an original mug-and-book task and diagrams.

reflection: Which crop lets you read the mug and book most easily?
Which margin or gap helped you decide?
Did your larger drawing keep the crop you chose?
extension: Try the same thumbnail test from a new viewpoint or with a different pair of simple objects. Notice how the crop changes the surrounding shapes.

teaching.whyItMatters: A few quick frame choices let you solve a composition while the mug and book are still simple shapes, before detail makes revision harder.
teaching.connections: Lesson 3 used negative shapes to check object edges. Here you compare those gaps inside a chosen frame, combining careful looking with a new composition decision; later still-life studies can revisit framing with more objects and less scaffolding.

deepDive: A frame does more than contain a drawing: its proportions and edges affect how large each object feels and where the surrounding spaces open or tighten. Thumbnail drawings make these relationships quick to compare. Keep them small and simple, and vary the crop or margins while the mug and book remain in the same arrangement. A thumbnail is a test of placement and shape balance, not a miniature finished picture.

As you compare, look at both the positive forms and the negative shapes between them, around their outlines, and beside the page edges. A narrow sliver where a book corner nearly touches the frame can create an accidental tangent, while a slightly wider crop may give that corner a clear margin. Sometimes an intentional crop can work too; the useful question is whether the edge reads clearly. Select a frame for the relationship it makes easiest to see, then carry that framing into a larger drawing and check it again.

Negative shapes are not filler: they share the same page with the objects, so a crop changes their balance even if the arrangement stays put. A tangent is a near-touch that can make two edges seem joined by accident. Widen a margin or cut more decisively only if a different frame still shows the mug-book relationship you meant to emphasize.

commonMistakes.mistake: Leaving a corner almost touching the frame edge by accident.
commonMistakes.lookFor: A very thin gap makes the book appear to merge with the frame or leaves an awkward sliver.
